text_blocks.snippet: Neutropenia, a condition characterized by low levels of neutrophils (a type of white blood cell), can be caused by a variety of medications. Some medications commonly associated with drug-induced neutropenia include certain antibiotics, antipsychotics, antiepileptics, antithyroid drugs, and antineoplastic agents.
snippet_highlighted_words: certain antibiotics, antipsychotics, antiepileptics, antithyroid drugs, and antineoplastic agents

list.title: Antibiotics:
list.snippet: Certain penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin, sulfonamides, and other antibiotics can induce neutropenia.

list.title: Antipsychotics:
list.snippet: Clozapine is a well-known culprit, but other antipsychotics may also be associated.

list.title: Antithyroid drugs:
list.snippet: Carbimazole and methimazole are examples of antithyroid medications linked to neutropenia.

list.title: Antineoplastic agents:
list.snippet: Chemotherapy drugs like doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, and cisplatin, as well as targeted therapies, can cause neutropenia.

list.title: Other medications:
list.snippet: Other medications, including some anti-seizure drugs, anti-fungal drugs, blood thinners (like ticlopidine), and rituximab (a monoclonal antibody), have also been associated with neutropenia.

list.title: Direct toxicity:
list.snippet: Some drugs can directly damage bone marrow cells responsible for producing neutrophils.

list.title: Immune-mediated reactions:
list.snippet: In other cases, the body's immune system may mistakenly attack neutrophils, leading to their destruction. This can involve the formation of antibodies that target neutrophils.
Drug-induced neutropenia is often idiosyncratic, meaning it occurs unpredictably in some individuals and not others.
Neutropenia can increase the risk of serious infections, as neutrophils play a crucial role in fighting off bacteria and fungi.
If you are taking any medications and experience symptoms of infection (e.g., fever, chills, sore throat), it's essential to seek medical attention promptly.
